# The divisor expansion {#sec-divisor}

This chapter explains the central arithmetic step in the paper's proof. As in @sec-second-moment, the original shape $\mathbf h$ is admissible. The problem left over is to evaluate the mixed moment $\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f)$, where $f(q)=f_{\mathbf h}(q)=\prod_{p\mid q}(1+c_p)$ is an arithmetic function of $q$ rather than a linear form.

## A product over primes is a sum over divisors

The distributive law turns $f(q)$ into a sum of simpler divisibility conditions.

For $q=30$, the prime divisors are $2,3,5$, so
$$
f(30)=(1+c_2)(1+c_3)(1+c_5).
$$
Choose either $1$ or $c_p$ from each parenthesis and multiply the choices. **Each selection of primes identifies a divisor:** $c_3c_5$ corresponds to $d=15$, while choosing $1$ throughout gives the term for $d=1$.

The table lists all eight choices. Its numerical column uses our shape $\mathbf h=(1,3)$, for which $c_2=0$, $c_3=1$ and $c_5=1/3$:

| Chosen primes | Divisor $d$ | Contribution $c(d)$ | Value for $\mathbf h=(1,3)$ |
|:--|--:|:--|:--:|
| None | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $2$ | $c_2$ | $0$ |
| $3$ | $3$ | $c_3$ | $1$ |
| $5$ | $5$ | $c_5$ | $1/3$ |
| $2,3$ | $6$ | $c_2c_3$ | $0$ |
| $2,5$ | $10$ | $c_2c_5$ | $0$ |
| $3,5$ | $15$ | $c_3c_5$ | $1/3$ |
| $2,3,5$ | $30$ | $c_2c_3c_5$ | $0$ |

Every contribution containing $c_2$ vanishes. The four remaining terms give
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(30)&=c(1)+c(3)+c(5)+c(15)\\
     &=1+1+\frac13+\frac13=\frac83.
\end{aligned}
$$
These are exact arithmetic values. The divisor sum contains the same contributions as the expanded product, now labelled by divisors.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Expanding all eight terms
Multiplying the first two parentheses gives
$$
(1+c_2)(1+c_3)=1+c_2+c_3+c_2c_3.
$$
Multiplying this by $1+c_5$ retains those four terms and adds a copy of each multiplied by $c_5$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
(1+c_2)(1+c_3)(1+c_5)
={}&1+c_2+c_3+c_2c_3\\
 &+c_5+c_2c_5+c_3c_5+c_2c_3c_5.
\end{aligned}
$$
The corresponding divisors are $1,2,3,6,5,10,15,30$. Reordering them gives the table above. Substituting $c_2=0$, $c_3=1$ and $c_5=1/3$ leaves the terms indexed by $1,3,5,15$, whose sum is $8/3$. Directly evaluating the product gives the same value:
$$
(1+0)(1+1)\left(1+\frac13\right)=\frac83.
$$
:::

For a general modulus, the product contains each **distinct** prime divisor once. Even if $3^2\mid q$, it still has only one factor $1+c_3$, so the expansion cannot produce $c_3^2$. The divisors obtained by choosing subsets of the prime divisors are therefore **squarefree**: no prime factor occurs twice. Defining
$$
c(d)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\prod_{p\mid d}c_p,&d\text{ squarefree},\\[4pt]
0,&d\text{ not squarefree},
\end{cases}
$$
lets us write the identity for every $q$:
$$
\boxed{f(q)=\prod_{p\mid q}(1+c_p)=\sum_{d\mid q}c(d).}
$$
Here $c(1)=1$, corresponding to choosing $1$ from every parenthesis. A squarefree divisor can also have coefficient zero, as the even divisors in the table show. Once the shape is fixed, every coefficient $c(d)$ is fixed; changing $q$ changes which divisors are included.

We can express that inclusion with the indicator $\mathbf1_{d\mid q}$, which is $1$ when $d$ divides $q$ and $0$ otherwise:
$$
f(q)=\sum_{d\ge1}c(d)\,\mathbf1_{d\mid q}.
$$
Substituting into the mixed moment and regrouping gives
$$
\boxed{
\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f)
=\sum_{d\le2Q}c(d)\,
  \mathbb E_w\bigl(U_\theta\mathbf1_{d\mid q}\bigr).
}
$$
Only $d\le2Q$ can occur because the moduli lie in $(Q,2Q]$. **Initially we take each modulus and list its divisors; after regrouping, we take each divisor and collect the moduli it divides.** The $d=3$ term collects contributions from multiples of $3$, and the $d=15$ term collects contributions from multiples of $15$.

These families overlap deliberately: $q=30$ contributes nonzero terms for $d=1,3,5,15$, with coefficients that add back to $f(30)=8/3$. Each restricted average retains the original denominator $D_Q=\sum_{Q<q\le2Q}q^2$ over all moduli. Thus the frequency of multiples of $d$ remains part of the calculation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Regrouping the weighted average without changing its normalisation
Recall that
$$
\mathbb E_w F=\frac1{D_Q}\sum_{Q<q\le2Q}q^2F(q).
$$
Substitute the divisor expansion into this finite sum:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f)
&=\frac1{D_Q}\sum_{Q<q\le2Q}
       q^2U_\theta(q)\sum_{d\mid q}c(d)\\
&=\sum_{d\le2Q}c(d)\left[
    \frac1{D_Q}\sum_{\substack{Q<q\le2Q\\d\mid q}}
       q^2U_\theta(q)\right].
\end{aligned}
$$
The quantity in brackets is exactly $\mathbb E_w(U_\theta\mathbf1_{d\mid q})$. The numerator receives contributions only from multiples of $d$, while the denominator is still the total weight over all moduli in the interval. Renormalising by the weight of the multiples alone would give a different average and would lose their frequency unless it were included separately.

Both sums are finite, so exchanging their order is exact. No estimate for the prime count has been used in this regrouping.
:::

This helps because **multiples of a fixed divisor form a linear family**. Hold $d$ fixed and write
$$
q=dn.
$$
The prime expressions become $a+h_jq=a+(dh_j)n$, still linear forms in the variables $(a,n)$. For example, $d=3$ turns our pair into
$$
a+3n,\qquad a+9n.
$$
As $q$ ranges over $(Q,2Q]$, the integer $n$ ranges over $(Q/d,2Q/d]$, and the starting-point range becomes $0<a\le\theta dn$.

The expansion has replaced one weight depending on all the prime divisors of $q$ by a sum of conditions $d\mid q$, each with a fixed coefficient $c(d)$. The following sections apply the Analytic Input when $d$ is small enough and control the contribution of the remaining divisors. Those estimates give the mixed moment its leading term $\theta G$, with the error control needed for the cancellation in @sec-second-moment. Up to this point, the product expansion and the regrouping have been exact.

## Multiples of $d$ are a linear change of variables

We now evaluate $\mathbb E_w(U_\theta\mathbf1_{d\mid q})$ for a fixed small divisor $d$. Writing $q=dn$ enforces divisibility and gives linear forms $a+(dh_j)n$. To apply the Analytic Input, we must also account for the weight in this average.

Recall that $C(q)=C_{\mathbf h}(q;\theta)$, $S=\mathfrak S(\mathbf h)$ and $U_\theta(q)=C(q)/(qS)$. The average $\mathbb E_w$ weights each modulus by $q^2$, so
$$
\mathbb E_w\bigl(U_\theta\mathbf1_{d\mid q}\bigr)
=\frac1{D_QS}\sum_{\substack{Q<q\le2Q\\d\mid q}}q\,C(q).
$$
One factor of $q$ cancels against the denominator in $U_\theta$, but **one factor of $q$ remains**. The normalising denominator $D_Q=\sum_{Q<q\le2Q}q^2$ still includes all moduli in the interval.

We reproduce that remaining factor by introducing an integer $b$ with $1\le b\le q=dn$. **Multiplying a contribution by $q$ is the same as adding it $q$ times.** Each of the $dn$ choices of $b$ contributes the same product of von Mangoldt weights, because none of the prime expressions depends on $b$.

For an exact example, take $\mathbf h=(1,3)$, $\theta=1$, $d=3$ and $n=2$, so $q=6$. The starting point $a=1$ gives the primes $7$ and $19$, contributing $(\log7)(\log19)$ to $C(6)$. Letting $b$ run through $1,\ldots,6$ gives
$$
\sum_{b=1}^{6}(\log7)(\log19)
=6(\log7)(\log19),
$$
exactly its contribution to $6C(6)$. Here $b$ labels repetitions of a numerical contribution. In the squared count in @sec-second-moment, $b$ was the starting point of a second prime pattern; here **there are still only $k$ prime expressions**, all depending on $n$ and $a$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Replacing the remaining weight by an extra sum
Substituting the definition of $U_\theta$ into the weighted average gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_w\bigl(U_\theta\mathbf1_{d\mid q}\bigr)
&=\frac1{D_Q}\sum_{\substack{Q<q\le2Q\\d\mid q}}
    q^2\frac{C(q)}{qS}\\
&=\frac1{D_QS}\sum_{\substack{Q<q\le2Q\\d\mid q}}qC(q).
\end{aligned}
$$
Now substitute $q=dn$ and expand $C(dn)$:
$$
\sum_{\substack{Q<q\le2Q\\d\mid q}}qC(q)
=\sum_{Q<dn\le2Q}dn
  \sum_{0<a\le\theta dn}\prod_{j=1}^k\Lambda(a+dh_jn).
$$
Since $dn=\sum_{b=1}^{dn}1$, this is exactly
$$
\sum_{\substack{Q<dn\le2Q\\
                0<a\le\theta dn\\
                0<b\le dn}}
\prod_{j=1}^k\Lambda(a+dh_jn).
$$
The extra sum accounts for the full remaining weight. No approximation has been made, and no primality condition is imposed on $b$.
:::

The numerator is now a sum of products of $\Lambda$ over three integer variables $(n,a,b)$ in the region
$$
\Omega_d=\bigl\{(n,a,b):\ Q<dn\le2Q,\
                  0<a\le\theta dn,\ 0<b\le dn\bigr\}.
$$
This is the form of sum evaluated by @thm-input: a volume times a product of local factors, with a controlled error. The region is convex, and no two forms $a+dh_jn$ have proportional coefficient vectors, because the lift indices are distinct. The fact that the forms do not depend on $b$ is permitted by the theorem.

The coefficient bound explains why we first restrict to small divisors. The permitted lift indices satisfy $h_j\le(\log Q)^B$. For a fixed $M$, taking
$$
d\le T:=(\log Q)^M
\qquad\text{gives}\qquad
dh_j\le(\log Q)^{B+M}.
$$
These coefficients remain polylogarithmic, within the Analytic Input's allowance. In each application, $d$ and the lift indices are fixed coefficients, while $n,a,b$ vary. The theorem's uniformity gives one error bound throughout this permitted family.

The volume is $\theta V_Q/d$, where $V_Q=\frac73Q^3$. The factor $\theta$ records the fraction of starting points being used, and $1/d$ reflects the spacing of the multiples of $d$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Checking the Analytic Input and computing the volume
The forms are
$$
\psi_j(n,a,b)=a+dh_jn,
$$
with coefficient vectors $(dh_j,1,0)$. If two such vectors were proportional, their coefficients of $a$ would force the proportionality factor to be $1$. Their coefficients of $n$ would then give $h_i=h_j$, contrary to distinctness. The system therefore satisfies the theorem's independence condition, with $m=3$ variables and $t=k$ forms.

The inequalities defining $\Omega_d$ are linear, so the region is convex. Since $d\ge1$ and $0\le\theta\le1$, it lies inside $[0,2Q]^3$, and all forms are positive on it. We can thus use an ambient size $N=2Q$ and a coefficient allowance covering $(\log Q)^{B+M}$.

At a fixed real value $n=x$, the allowed $(a,b)$ form a rectangle with side lengths $\theta dx$ and $dx$. Its area is $\theta d^2x^2$. Integrating these areas gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{vol}(\Omega_d)
&=\int_{Q/d}^{2Q/d}\theta d^2x^2\,dx\\
&=\frac{\theta}{d}\int_Q^{2Q}y^2\,dy\\
&=\frac{\theta}{d}\,\frac73Q^3
=\frac{\theta V_Q}{d}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The substitution in the second line is $y=dx$. Also,
$$
D_Q=\sum_{Q<q\le2Q}q^2=V_Q+O(Q^2),
$$
so dividing the volume by $D_Q$ gives $\theta/d$ to leading order.
:::

It remains to identify the arithmetic correction. At each prime $p$, the fixed divisor $d$ determines which local calculation applies:

- If $p\mid d$, then $q=dn$ is forced to be $0$ modulo $p$. Every form reduces to $a$, so the local factor is $t_p$.
- If $p\nmid d$, multiplication by $d$ permutes the residues modulo $p$. As $n$ runs through its residues, $q=dn$ runs through all residues, giving the average factor $A_p$ from @sec-second-moment. This includes $q\equiv0\pmod p$, which occurs when $n\equiv0\pmod p$.

The unrestricted residue of $b$ leaves these local factors unchanged: every passing choice of $(n,a)$ has all $p$ choices of $b$, and the additional factor $p$ cancels in the residue average.

The full correction is
$$
\mathfrak U_d=\prod_{p\mid d}t_p\prod_{p\nmid d}A_p.
$$

The Analytic Input gives the numerator the leading term $(\theta V_Q/d)\mathfrak U_d$. Dividing by $D_QS$, with $D_Q\sim V_Q$, gives
$$
\mathbb E_w\bigl(U_\theta\,\mathbf1_{d\mid q}\bigr)
=\frac{\theta\,\mathfrak U_d}{d\,\mathfrak S(\mathbf h)}
 +O\bigl((\log Q)^{-E}\bigr)
\qquad(d\le T).
$$
Once $M$ is fixed, the Analytic Input lets us make the error exponent $E$ as large as needed. We have therefore evaluated each contribution from a small divisor, retaining both its frequency through $1/d$ and its divisibility restrictions through $\mathfrak U_d$. The next section controls the remaining divisors before we combine the contributions to obtain the mixed moment.

## Truncate by the size of the divisor, not by the size of the primes

The preceding section evaluates the contribution of each divisor $d\le T=(\log Q)^M$. We now justify keeping only those contributions by proving that the combined effect of the omitted terms is small. To **truncate** the divisor sum means to write
$$
f(q)=f_T(q)+r_T(q),
$$
where
$$
f_T(q)=\sum_{\substack{d\mid q\\d\le T}}c(d),
\qquad
r_T(q)=\sum_{\substack{d\mid q\\d>T}}c(d).
$$
The remainder $r_T=f-f_T$ is called the **tail**. We still average over all moduli in $(Q,2Q]$; the cutoff selects which divisor contributions we retain within each $f(q)$.

The size of the whole divisor matters because writing $q=dn$ gives the prime expressions $a+(dh_j)n$. Their coefficients involve $d$ itself. A product of several small primes can already be too large for the coefficient bound we have chosen.

Return to $q=30$ and $\mathbf h=(1,3)$. The nonzero contributions have $d=1,3,5,15$. With a divisor cutoff $T=5$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(30)&=1+1+\frac13+\frac13=\frac83,\\
f_5(30)&=1+1+\frac13=\frac73.
\end{aligned}
$$
The omitted contribution is $r_5(30)=c(15)=1/3$. **Both prime factors of $15$ are at most $5$, but their product exceeds $5$.** A cutoff retaining every prime up to $5$ would keep the factors $1+c_3$ and $1+c_5$, and therefore also their cross-term $c_3c_5=c(15)$. It would retain the full value $8/3$ in this example. The two cutoffs select different terms.

More generally, the product of distinct primes up to $z$ can be as large as the **primorial**
$$
P(z):=\prod_{p\le z}p,
$$
which grows roughly like $e^z$. Conditioning on $q$ modulo $P(z)$ to handle all these divisibility conditions together introduces coefficients of this size. Keeping them within a fixed power of $\log Q$ would restrict $z$ to $O(\log\log Q)$. A tail estimate decreasing as an inverse power of $z$ would then give only an inverse power of $\log\log Q$, slower than the prescribed inverse powers of $\log Q$ needed in the proof.

A divisor cutoff directly controls the relevant coefficients:
$$
d\le T=(\log Q)^M
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
dh_j\le(\log Q)^{B+M}.
$$
It discards both large prime divisors and products of smaller primes whose product exceeds $T$. We must bound their combined contribution.

**Rankin's trick extracts a small factor from every omitted term.** Fix $0<\delta<1$. If $d>T$, then $(d/T)^\delta>1$. Multiplying the nonnegative term $c(d)$ by this quantity makes it larger. Applying this to the tail and then adding the remaining nonnegative terms gives
$$
r_T(q)\le T^{-\delta}F_\delta(q),
\qquad
F_\delta(q):=\prod_{p\mid q}(1+c_pp^\delta).
$$
The gain is the explicit factor $T^{-\delta}$. The remaining product has a bounded average square. The proof uses the bound $c_p\ll_k1/p$ together with the small frequency of divisibility by large primes. The calculation below makes this precise.

Consequently, the **root-mean-square size** of the tail satisfies
$$
\boxed{
\|r_T\|_{L^2(w)}
=\sqrt{\mathbb E_w\bigl(r_T(q)^2\bigr)}
\ll_{k,\delta}T^{-\delta}.
}
$$
This is control on average over moduli, with the same $q^2$ weights as before. Individual moduli can have larger tails.

This bound gives the logarithmic accuracy needed for the mixed moment. Choose $\delta=1/2$ and $T=(\log Q)^M$. Then
$$
\|r_T\|_{L^2(w)}\ll_k(\log Q)^{-M/2}.
$$
For any desired exponent $R>0$, taking $M=2R$ makes this at most a constant times $(\log Q)^{-R}$. The coefficients $dh_j$ remain bounded by a fixed power of $\log Q$, so the retained terms are still covered by the Analytic Input.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Rankin's trick
For every omitted divisor $d>T$, the inequality $1<(d/T)^\delta$ and the nonnegativity of $c(d)$ give
$$
\begin{aligned}
0\le r_T(q)
&=\sum_{\substack{d\mid q\\d>T}}c(d)\\
&\le T^{-\delta}\sum_{\substack{d\mid q\\d>T}}c(d)d^\delta\\
&\le T^{-\delta}\sum_{d\mid q}c(d)d^\delta\\
&=T^{-\delta}\prod_{p\mid q}(1+c_pp^\delta)
=T^{-\delta}F_\delta(q).
\end{aligned}
$$
The second inequality adds the terms with $d\le T$. The last equality is the product-to-divisor-sum identity from Section 6.1, now with prime coefficients $c_pp^\delta$.

To bound the average square of $F_\delta$, expand
$$
F_\delta(q)^2
=\prod_{p\mid q}\bigl(1+2c_pp^\delta+c_p^2p^{2\delta}\bigr)
=\sum_{d\mid q}b_\delta(d).
$$
Here $b_\delta(d)$ is nonnegative, supported on squarefree divisors, and multiplicative, with
$$
b_\delta(p)=2c_pp^\delta+c_p^2p^{2\delta}.
$$
The weighted frequency of multiples obeys $\mathbb E_w\mathbf1_{d\mid q}\ll1/d$ for $d\le2Q$ and is zero for larger $d$. Expanding first and then averaging therefore gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_wF_\delta(q)^2
&=\sum_{d\le2Q}b_\delta(d)\,
     \mathbb E_w\mathbf1_{d\mid q}\\
&\ll\sum_{d\ge1}\frac{b_\delta(d)}d\\
&=\prod_p\left(1+\frac{b_\delta(p)}p\right).
\end{aligned}
$$
The factor $1/p$ in the product reflects the frequency of divisibility by $p$. Since $c_p\ll_k1/p$,
$$
\frac{b_\delta(p)}p
\ll_k p^{\delta-2}+p^{2\delta-3}.
$$
For $\delta<1$, both exponents are less than $-1$, so the sums of these bounds over primes converge. For example, $\delta=1/2$ gives $p^{-3/2}+p^{-2}$. Thus
$$
\mathbb E_wF_\delta(q)^2\ll_{k,\delta}1,
$$
uniformly in $Q$ and the admissible shape. This is where the restriction $\delta<1$ enters: the initial pointwise inequality holds for every positive $\delta$, while this convergence argument requires $\delta<1$.

Squaring the pointwise bound and averaging now yields
$$
\mathbb E_w r_T(q)^2
\le T^{-2\delta}\mathbb E_wF_\delta(q)^2
\ll_{k,\delta}T^{-2\delta}.
$$
Taking square roots proves $\|r_T\|_{L^2(w)}\ll_{k,\delta}T^{-\delta}$.
:::

To see how the tail affects the mixed moment, apply Cauchy--Schwarz:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f)-\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f_T)\right|
&=\left|\mathbb E_w(U_\theta r_T)\right|\\
&\le\|U_\theta\|_{L^2(w)}\,\|r_T\|_{L^2(w)}\\
&\ll_{k,\delta}T^{-\delta}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The earlier second-moment estimate bounds $\|U_\theta\|_{L^2(w)}$; Rankin's trick bounds the other factor. Thus the error introduced by omitting the large divisors can be made as small as any prescribed inverse power of $\log Q$.

The preceding section evaluates the retained terms, and this section controls the omitted terms. The next section combines them to evaluate the full mixed moment. @fig-tail illustrates the convergence of the arithmetic partial sums in a finite-prime version of that calculation; the solid curve corresponds to the mixed moment and the dotted curve to the first moment of $f$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tail
#| fig-pos: H
#| fig-cap: "For $\\mathbf h=(1,3)$: finite-prime versions of the mixed-moment partial sums (solid) and the first-moment partial sums $\\sum_{d\\le T}c(d)/d$ (dotted). Every product is restricted to primes $p\\le3000$, and only divisors composed of these primes are included, up to $T=20000$. The dashed lines are the corresponding finite products $G_{\\le3000}=\\prod_{p\\le3000}(1+(2c_p+c_p^2)/p)$ and $H_{\\le3000}=\\prod_{p\\le3000}(1+c_p/p)$."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from helpers import PRIMES, c_p, BLUE, RUST, GREEN
h = (1,3); P = [int(p) for p in PRIMES if p <= 3000]
cp = {p: c_p(h,p) for p in P}
G = np.prod([1 + (2*cp[p] + cp[p]**2)/p for p in P]); Ef = np.prod([1 + cp[p]/p for p in P])
prodA = np.prod([1 + cp[p]/p for p in P])            # prod_p A_p/S_p
# squarefree d <= Tmax built from primes with c_p > 0
Tmax = 20000; terms = {1: 1.0}
for p in P:
    if cp[p] == 0 or p > Tmax: continue
    for d, v in list(terms.items()):
        if d*p <= Tmax: terms[d*p] = v*cp[p]
ds = np.array(sorted(terms)); cd = np.array([terms[d] for d in ds])
def U_over_S(d):
    r = prodA
    m = d
    for p in P:
        if m % p == 0: r *= (1 + cp[p])/(1 + cp[p]/p)
    return r
mixed = np.cumsum(cd*np.array([U_over_S(int(d)) for d in ds])/ds); mean = np.cumsum(cd/ds)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.plot(ds, mixed, color=BLUE, lw=2, label="mixed-moment partial sums"); ax.axhline(G, color=BLUE, ls="--", lw=1, label="$G_{\\leq3000}$")
ax.plot(ds, mean, color=GREEN, lw=2, ls=":", label="$\\sum_{d\\leq T} c(d)/d$"); ax.axhline(Ef, color=GREEN, ls="--", lw=1, label="$H_{\\leq3000}$")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("$T$"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout()
```

## The Euler product closes

We can now complete the task left open in @sec-second-moment: prove that the mixed moment has the same arithmetic factor $G$ as the two second moments. Recall that $S=\mathfrak S(\mathbf h)$, $U_\theta(q)=C_{\mathbf h}(q;\theta)/(qS)$, and the predicted value of $U_\theta(q)$ is $\theta f(q)$.

The preceding sections reduce the mixed moment to an arithmetic sum:
$$
\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f)
\approx\theta\sum_{d\ge1}\frac{c(d)\,\mathfrak U_d}{dS}.
$$
Here $\mathfrak U_d$ is the arithmetic correction for moduli restricted to multiples of $d$. The approximation has controlled errors from the Analytic Input and from the omitted divisors. Our next step is to evaluate the displayed arithmetic sum exactly.

**Each prime contributes according to whether we include it in the divisor $d$.** Only squarefree divisors have nonzero coefficients. For each included prime, $c(d)/d$ supplies $c_p/p$. The correction $\mathfrak U_d/S$ supplies $t_p/S_p$ at included primes and $A_p/S_p$ at omitted primes.

Omitting $p$ from $d$ leaves $q$ unrestricted modulo $p$: the variable $n$ in $q=dn$ may still be divisible by $p$. This gives the average correction $A_p$. Including $p$ in $d$ forces $p\mid q$, giving $t_p$. The two choices therefore contribute:

| Choice for the divisor $d$ | Contribution at $p$ |
|:--|:--|
| Omit $p$ | $\displaystyle\frac{A_p}{S_p}=1+\frac{c_p}{p}$ |
| Include $p$ | $\displaystyle\frac{c_p}{p}\frac{t_p}{S_p}=\frac{c_p(1+c_p)}p$ |

For example, the term indexed by $d=15$ chooses the second row at $3$ and $5$, and the first row at every other prime. Summing over all squarefree $d$ adds together all such finite selections. **The distributive law, read in reverse, turns this sum of choices into a product of their sums:**
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{d\ge1}\frac{c(d)\,\mathfrak U_d}{dS}
&=\prod_p\left(\frac{A_p}{S_p}
                 +\frac{c_pt_p}{pS_p}\right)\\
&=\prod_p\left(1+\frac{2c_p+c_p^2}{p}\right)
=G.
\end{aligned}
$$
A product with one factor for each prime is called an **Euler product**. The convergence and tail estimates justifying this identity are given in the callout below.

To see why this is the same $G$ as before, return to the second-moment calculation. The local correction divided by $S_p$ is $1$ when $p\nmid q$ and $1+c_p$ when $p\mid q$. Averaging its square over the residues of $q$ modulo $p$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{B_p}{S_p^2}
&=\left(1-\frac1p\right)1^2+\frac1p(1+c_p)^2\\
&=1+\frac{2c_p+c_p^2}{p}.
\end{aligned}
$$
This is exactly the factor obtained from the divisor sum. The same calculation gives the local average for $f(q)^2$, whose factor is also $1$ or $(1+c_p)^2$ according to the divisibility of $q$. **The squared count, the mixed moment, and the squared multiplier therefore produce the same arithmetic factor at every prime.**

Our familiar example modulo $3$ makes the match concrete. For $\mathbf h=(1,3)$, we have $S_3=3/4$, $t_3=3/2$, $A_3=1$ and $c_3=1$. Organising the calculation by the choice of divisor, or by the residue of $q$, gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Divisor expansion:}\quad&
\underbrace{\frac{A_3}{S_3}}_{3\nmid d}
+\underbrace{\frac{c_3t_3}{3S_3}}_{3\mid d}
=\frac43+\frac23=2,\\[8pt]
\text{Second moment:}\quad&
\underbrace{\frac23}_{3\nmid q}\,1^2
+\underbrace{\frac13}_{3\mid q}\,2^2
=2.
\end{aligned}
$$
These are two exact arithmetic calculations of the same local factor. The full $G$ multiplies the corresponding factors at all primes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Factoring the sum and controlling its tail
For squarefree $d$, combine the definitions of $c(d)$, $\mathfrak U_d$ and $S$:
$$
\frac{c(d)\mathfrak U_d}{dS}
=\prod_{p\nmid d}\frac{A_p}{S_p}
 \prod_{p\mid d}\frac{c_pt_p}{pS_p}.
$$
Extract the fixed baseline
$$
H_0:=\prod_p\frac{A_p}{S_p}
=\prod_p\left(1+\frac{c_p}{p}\right).
$$
Then
$$
\frac{c(d)\mathfrak U_d}{dS}
=H_0\prod_{p\mid d}\frac{c_pt_p}{pA_p}.
$$
The remaining coefficients are multiplicative and supported on squarefree integers. Summing their products over all squarefree $d$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{d\ge1}\frac{c(d)\mathfrak U_d}{dS}
&=H_0\prod_p\left(1+\frac{c_pt_p}{pA_p}\right)\\
&=\prod_p\left(\frac{A_p}{S_p}
                  +\frac{c_pt_p}{pS_p}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$
For finitely many prime choices this is the distributive law. The infinite identity follows by convergence: $H_0$ is bounded because $c_p/p\ll_kp^{-2}$, and the remaining prime coefficients satisfy
$$
\frac{c_pt_p}{pA_p}
=\frac{c_p(1+c_p)}{p(1+c_p/p)}
\ll_k p^{-2}.
$$
Multiplying these prime coefficients by $p^\delta$ still gives a convergent prime sum for $0<\delta<1$. Rankin's argument therefore bounds the omitted part of the arithmetic series:
$$
\sum_{d>T}\frac{c(d)\mathfrak U_d}{dS}
\ll_{k,\delta}T^{-\delta}.
$$
There are two truncations to remove. This bound replaces the truncated arithmetic series by its full value $G$. The Cauchy--Schwarz estimate in the preceding section replaces $\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f_T)$ by $\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f)$ with an error of the same order. Combining these bounds with the summed analytic error gives
$$
\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f)
=\theta G+O_{k,B,M,R_1,\delta}
 \bigl(L^{-R_1}+T^{-\delta}\bigr),
$$
where $L=\log Q$ and $R_1$ is the chosen exponent for the analytic error after summing over $d\le T$. The cutoff is $T=L^M$, so it grows with $Q$ while staying within the allowed coefficient range.
:::

This proves the missing mixed-moment estimate. Together with @sec-second-moment, we now have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_wU_\theta^2&\approx\theta^2G,\\
\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f)&\approx\theta G,\\
\mathbb E_wf^2&\approx G.
\end{aligned}
$$
The exact identity for the squared prediction error is
$$
\mathbb E_w|U_\theta-\theta f|^2
=\mathbb E_wU_\theta^2
 -2\theta\,\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f)
 +\theta^2\mathbb E_wf^2.
$$
Substituting the three leading terms produces
$$
\theta^2G-2\theta(\theta G)+\theta^2G=0.
$$
**The leading arithmetic terms cancel; the errors in their estimates remain.** The mixed moment supplies the middle term with precisely the size needed for that cancellation. Its value has been established by the restricted-count estimates and the divisor calculation above.

The remaining errors can be bounded by any prescribed inverse power of $\log Q$. We first choose a sufficiently large fixed power $T=(\log Q)^M$ to control the tails, then ask the Analytic Input for enough accuracy to handle the sum of the retained terms. This gives
$$
\mathbb E_w|U_\theta-\theta f|^2\ll(\log Q)^{-R}
$$
for any fixed $R>0$, uniformly in the permitted admissible shapes and in $\theta$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Tracking the errors and choosing the parameters
Write the three estimates with their errors:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_wU_\theta^2&=\theta^2G+\varepsilon_1,\\
\mathbb E_w(U_\theta f)&=\theta G+\varepsilon_2,\\
\mathbb E_wf^2&=G+\varepsilon_3.
\end{aligned}
$$
Substitution into the exact squared-error identity leaves
$$
\mathbb E_w|U_\theta-\theta f|^2
=\varepsilon_1-2\theta\varepsilon_2+\theta^2\varepsilon_3.
$$
The errors can have either sign, but the squared error is nonnegative. Thus
$$
0\le\mathbb E_w|U_\theta-\theta f|^2
\le |\varepsilon_1|+2\theta|\varepsilon_2|
   +\theta^2|\varepsilon_3|.
$$
With $L=\log Q$, the resulting bound is
$$
\mathbb E_w|U_\theta-\theta f|^2
\ll L^{-R_1}+T^{-\delta}+Q^{-1/2}.
$$
The first term comes from the analytic estimates, the second from truncation, and the third from averaging the arithmetic multiplier $f^2$. For a desired bound $O(L^{-R})$, take
$$
\delta=\frac12,\qquad
M=2(R+1),\qquad
R_1=R+1.
$$
Then $T^{-\delta}=L^{-(R+1)}$, and $Q^{-1/2}$ is eventually smaller than any fixed inverse power of $L$.

Once $M$ is fixed, choose the Analytic Input's coefficient allowance to cover $B+M$. Its error exponent must also allow for summation over $d\le T$. Since $c(d)\ll_k1$, summing errors of order $L^{-E}$ over at most $T=L^M$ divisors costs at most a factor of $L^M$. For example, $E>R_1+M+2$ suffices. This order of choices keeps every coefficient polylogarithmic and makes the combined error $O(L^{-R})$.
:::

Finally, return to normalisation by the full singular series. Since
$$
\frac{U_\theta(q)}{f(q)}
=\frac{C_{\mathbf h}(q;\theta)}{q\,\mathfrak S(q\mathbf h)}
$$
and $f(q)\ge1$, dividing the discrepancy by $f(q)$ cannot enlarge it:
$$
\left|\frac{U_\theta(q)}{f(q)}-\theta\right|
=\frac{|U_\theta(q)-\theta f(q)|}{f(q)}
\le |U_\theta(q)-\theta f(q)|.
$$
We obtain
$$
\boxed{
\mathbb E_w\left|
\frac{C_{\mathbf h}(q;\theta)}{q\,\mathfrak S(q\mathbf h)}-\theta
\right|^2\ll(\log Q)^{-R}.
}
$$
The target is $\theta$, and is $1$ when the whole starting-point interval is used. The small mean-square error implies accuracy for most moduli by Section 5.1; the comparability of the weights transfers this conclusion to the uniform average. These are still von Mangoldt weighted counts. @sec-one-set constructs the common exceptional set and removes the prime-power contributions and logarithmic weights to recover the prime-tuple count.

::: {.callout-important}
## The idea in one sentence
Averaging the prime count against an arithmetic weight $f(q)$ is hard, but $f$ is a nonnegative weighted sum of divisibility indicators, and averaging a prime count along multiples of a fixed small $d$ is another linear-equations problem. The resulting Euler product is the same $G$ that governs the second moment, so the leading terms of the mean-square error cancel exactly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where this is in the paper
Section 3 is this chapter. Lemma 3.1 is the tail bound and the second moment of $f$; Proposition 3.2 proves the prime-count mean-square estimate using the mixed-moment computation. The dummy-variable body is display (24), the local factor $\mathfrak U_d$ is just below it, and the Euler identity is display (27). Remark 3.3 explains why the truncation is by divisor size.
:::
